title: Emergence of Hierarchical Emotion Organization in Large Language Models
claim: A hierarchy of categories recovered from a model's outputs closely mirrors the human-annotated expert taxonomy.
layout: 2 side-by-side sunburst panels, left-to-right, matched color palette across panels
description: Two circular sunburst charts sit side by side. Panel (a), titled 'Shaver et al., 1987' in blue, shows the human-annotated emotion wheel. Six core emotions form the inner ring: fear, love, joy, surprise, anger and sadness. Dozens of finer-grained emotion words fill a dense outer ring, with tiny rotated labels. Panel (b), titled 'Llama 405B', shows the hierarchy reconstructed from the model. It has the same color-coded palette running from purple and blue through green, yellow, orange and red. The inner ring has fewer categories, such as fear, sadness, happiness and anger. The outer words are fewer and sit at uneven radial lengths, so some segments stick out as spikes. The eye goes first to the large colorful wheels and then compares their structure. The matching colors suggest the model's structure agrees with the human one.
caption: Emotion wheel. (a) Human-annotated emotion wheel proposed by [ref], widely used in cognitive science. (b) Hierarchy of emotions reconstructed from Llama 405B.
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) increasingly power conversational agents, understanding how they model users' emotional states is critical for ethical deployment. Inspired by emotion wheels, i.e., a psychological framework that argues emotions organize hierarchically, we analyze probabilistic dependencies between emotional states in model outputs. We find that LLMs naturally form hierarchical emotion trees that align with human psychological models, and larger models develop more complex hierarchies. We also uncover systematic biases in emotion recognition across socioeconomic personas, with compounding misclassifications for intersectional, underrepresented groups. Human studies reveal striking parallels, suggesting that LLMs internalize aspects of social perception. Beyond highlighting emergent emotional reasoning in LLMs, our results hint at the potential of using cognitively-grounded theories for developing better model evaluations.
